sources.entry: Writing a Good CLAUDE.md by HumanLayer - An essay on CLAUDE.md craft: instruction-budget reasoning, progressive disclosure, and the test of whether Claude would err without a given line.

summary.name: Writing a good CLAUDE.md
summary.one_liner: An essay by HumanLayer's Kyle giving practical guidance on writing CLAUDE.md (and AGENTS.md) files that onboard coding agents like Claude Code to a codebase.
use_cases: Writing a CLAUDE.md file for a new repository
Reducing instructions that coding agents ignore
Structuring agent docs for a monorepo
Deciding whether to use linters or hooks instead of agent instructions
Setting up progressive disclosure for agent context
summary.what_it_does: The essay explains that LLM coding agents are stateless and only know what is in the context, so CLAUDE.md (loaded into every session) should cover WHAT (stack and project map), WHY (purpose of parts of the project), and HOW (commands, tests, verification). It argues for keeping instructions few and universally applicable, citing rough research on instruction-following decay and a claim about Claude Code's system prompt containing about 50 instructions. It recommends progressive disclosure: keep task-specific docs in separate markdown files and point to them with file:line references instead of code snippets. It also advises against using the agent as a linter, suggesting deterministic tools and Stop hooks, and against auto-generating CLAUDE.md with /init.
notable: Progressive disclosure approach using separate agent_docs markdown files referenced from CLAUDE.md
Argues that Claude may ignore CLAUDE.md because Claude Code wraps it with a 'may or may not be relevant' system reminder
Recommends delegating formatting and style checks to linters and Stop hooks rather than instructions
Says HumanLayer's root CLAUDE.md is under sixty lines
caveats: Guidance is based on the author's reasoning and limited research; the page itself says mileage may vary and the topic is not rigorously investigated
Page states Anthropic gives no official length recommendation; the under-300-lines figure is described as general consensus
